lessons.title: More Precise Targeting
lessons.content: Beyond basic class and ID selectors, CSS offers more advanced selectors to target elements with incredible precision.

lessons.title: Descendant Selector
lessons.content:
A space between selectors targets a descendant. For example, `article p` selects any `

` that is somewhere inside an `

`.

lessons.title: Select all links `<a>` that are inside a `nav` element.
Child Selector
lessons.content: The `>` combinator selects a direct child. `ul > li` selects only `<li>` elements that are direct children of a `<ul>`, not those nested deeper.

lessons.title: Select only the direct `p` children of a `div` with the class 'card'.

lessons.question: What does `div > p` select?
options: A p that is a direct child of a div
A p that is a parent of a div
lessons.correct: A p that is a direct child of a div

lessons.title: Adjacent Sibling Selector
lessons.content:
The `+` combinator selects an element that is immediately after another specific element. `h1 + p` selects the first `

` right after an `

`.

lessons.title: Give the paragraph immediately following an `h2` some top margin.

lessons.instruction: Select the `<span>` that is a direct child of the `<strong>` tag.

lessons.title: Selector Sensei! 🥋
lessons.content: You can now target elements with surgical precision. This is key to writing clean CSS that doesn't require adding extra classes to everything.

lessons.title: Styling by Attribute
lessons.content: Attribute selectors allow you to select elements based on the presence or value of their HTML attributes.

lessons.title: Presence Selector
lessons.content: The `[attribute]` syntax selects any element that has the specified attribute, regardless of its value. `[required]` selects any element with the `required` attribute.

lessons.title: Select all `<a>` tags that have a `target` attribute.
Exact Value Selector
lessons.content: The `[attribute='value']` syntax selects elements where the attribute has a specific, exact value. `[type='submit']` selects only submit buttons.

lessons.title: Select only links that go to 'https://example.com'.

lessons.question: How do you select an input with the exact type 'checkbox'?

lessons.title: Substring Selectors
lessons.content: You can also select based on substrings in an attribute's value. `[class*='icon-']` selects elements whose class contains 'icon-' anywhere inside it.

lessons.title: Select all links whose `href` attribute begins with 'https'.

lessons.instruction: Select all `` tags whose `src` attribute ends with '.png'.

lessons.title: Attribute Authority! 🏷️
lessons.content: You've unlocked a powerful way to style elements without needing to add extra classes, leading to cleaner HTML and more flexible CSS.

lessons.title: Beyond Hover and Active
lessons.content: Pseudo-classes let you style elements based on their state or position in the document tree. Let's explore some more advanced ones.

lessons.title: Positional Pseudo-Classes
lessons.content: `:first-child` selects an element that is the first child of its parent. `:last-child` selects the last one.

lessons.title: Remove the top border from the first list item in any list.

lessons.question: Which pseudo-class targets the last paragraph inside a div?

lessons.title: The `:nth-child` Selector
lessons.content: `:nth-child(n)` is incredibly powerful. You can pass it a number (`2`), a keyword (`odd` or `even`), or a formula (`2n+1`) to select specific children.

lessons.title: Give every even row in a table a light grey background (zebra-striping).
UI State Pseudo-Classes
lessons.content: Pseudo-classes like `:checked` (for checkboxes/radios), `:disabled`, and `:focus` (for inputs) let you style elements based on their interaction state.

lessons.title: Add a blue outline to any input field when it is focused.

lessons.instruction: Select the third `<li>` element in a list.

lessons.title: State Stylist! ✨
lessons.content: You can now write CSS that responds to the structure of your document and the state of your UI, making your designs more robust and interactive.

lessons.title: Styling Virtual Elements
lessons.content: Pseudo-elements create abstractions of the document tree that can be styled. They are prefixed with `::`.

lessons.title: Decorating with `::before` and `::after`
lessons.content: These are the most common pseudo-elements. They insert generated content before or after an element's actual content. They require a `content` property.

lessons.title: Add a quotation mark before every `<blockquote>`.

lessons.question: Which property is required for `::before` and `::after` to work?

lessons.title: Styling the First Line and Letter
lessons.content: `::first-line` applies styles to the first line of a block-level element. `::first-letter` applies styles to the first letter, creating a 'drop cap' effect.

lessons.title: Make the first letter of every article's first paragraph larger and bolder.
Styling Form Selections
lessons.content: The `::selection` pseudo-element applies styles to the part of a document that has been highlighted by the user (e.g., by clicking and dragging).

lessons.title: Change the background color of user-selected text to gold.
Virtual Virtuoso! 🎩
lessons.content: You've mastered the art of styling parts of the document that don't exist in the HTML. This is an elegant way to add decoration and polish.

lessons.title: Reusable Values
lessons.content: CSS variables, also known as Custom Properties, allow you to define reusable values (like colors or sizes) in one place and reference them throughout your stylesheet.

lessons.title: Declaring Variables
lessons.content: You declare a variable on a selector (often `:root` to make it global) using a name that starts with two hyphens, like `--main-color: #333;`.

lessons.title: Declare a global CSS variable named `--primary-font` and set it to 'Arial'.

lessons.question: What must a CSS variable name start with?

lessons.title: Using Variables
lessons.content: You use a variable with the `var()` function, like `color: var(--main-color);`.

lessons.title: Declare a main color variable and then use it on the `body`'s background.
Fallback Values
lessons.content: The `var()` function can take a second argument, which is a fallback value to use if the variable is not defined.

lessons.title: Use a variable for font size, but provide '16px' as a fallback.
Theme Architect! 🏗️
lessons.content: CSS variables are the cornerstone of modern theming (e.g., light/dark mode) and creating scalable, maintainable design systems. Great job!

lessons.title: Calculations in CSS
lessons.content: The `calc()` function lets you perform mathematical calculations right inside your CSS property values.

lessons.title: Mixing Units
lessons.content: The true power of `calc()` is its ability to mix different units, like percentages and pixels, which is impossible otherwise.

lessons.title: Set the width of an element to be 100% of its parent, minus 20 pixels.

lessons.question: What is the main benefit of `calc()`?

lessons.title: Syntax Note
lessons.content: It's important to have spaces around the operators (+, -, *, /) inside `calc()`.

lessons.question: Which syntax is correct?

lessons.title: Set an element's height to be the full viewport height minus the 60px header.
Using with Variables
lessons.content: `calc()` works beautifully with CSS variables, allowing for highly dynamic and configurable layouts.

lessons.title: Set a font size to be a base variable plus 2 pixels.
CSS Calculator! 🧮
lessons.content: You can now create fluid layouts that perfectly adapt to fixed elements, a common challenge in web design. This is a very practical skill.

lessons.title: Manipulating Space
lessons.content: The `transform` property lets you modify the coordinate space of an element, allowing you to translate (move), rotate, scale, and skew it.

lessons.title: Translate
lessons.content: The `translate()` function moves an element from its current position. `transform: translate(50px, 20px)` moves it 50px right and 20px down.

lessons.title: Move an element 100 pixels to the right.
Rotate
lessons.content: The `rotate()` function rotates an element around its center. It takes an angle value, like `deg` for degrees.

lessons.question: Which function would you use to spin an element?

lessons.title: Scale
lessons.content: The `scale()` function resizes an element. `scale(2)` makes it twice as big, while `scale(0.5)` makes it half the size.

lessons.title: Make a button grow to 1.1 times its size on hover.

lessons.instruction: Combine a scale and a rotation transform.

lessons.title: Space Bender! 💫
lessons.content: You can now manipulate elements in 2D space, which is the foundation for creating engaging micro-interactions and animations.

lessons.title: Adding Depth
lessons.content: 3D transforms add a Z-axis to your manipulations, allowing you to create effects with perspective and depth.

lessons.title: The `perspective` Property
lessons.content: To enable a 3D space, the *parent* element needs a `perspective` property. This defines how intense the 3D effect is (lower values are more extreme).

lessons.title: Create a 3D space on a container element.
3D Rotate
lessons.content: You can now rotate elements around the X, Y, or Z axes. `rotateX(45deg)` tilts an element back, while `rotateY(45deg)` turns it sideways.

lessons.title: Flip a card over by rotating it 180 degrees on the Y-axis.

lessons.question: Which rotation would make an element look like it's falling backward into the screen?

lessons.title: 3D Translate
lessons.content: `translateZ()` moves an element closer to or further away from the viewer along the Z-axis, making it appear larger or smaller.

lessons.title: Move an element 100 pixels 'closer' to the viewer.
Creating a 3D Cube
lessons.content: By combining these properties on multiple faces of an object, you can create fully 3D shapes like cubes directly in CSS.

lessons.title: Dimension Drifter! 🧊
lessons.content: You've unlocked the third dimension! This allows for stunning visual effects like card flips, 3D carousels, and much more.

lessons.title: Smoother Animations
lessons.content: The `transition` property animates an element smoothly from one state to another. Let's explore its sub-properties for more control.

lessons.title: Sub-properties
lessons.content: The `transition` shorthand combines `transition-property`, `transition-duration`, `transition-timing-function`, and `transition-delay`.

lessons.title: Create a transition that only animates the `background-color` property over 0.5 seconds.
Timing Functions
lessons.content: The `transition-timing-function` controls the acceleration curve. Common values are `ease` (default), `linear`, `ease-in`, `ease-out`, and `ease-in-out`.

lessons.title: Make a box slide in slowly and then speed up.
lessons.expectedAnswer:
.box { transform: translateX(-100%); transition: transform 1s ease-in; }
.box.active { transform: translateX(0); }
blocks:
.box { transform: translateX(-100%); transition: transform 1s ease-in; }
.box.active { transform: translateX(0); }

lessons.question: Which timing function has no acceleration or deceleration?

lessons.title: Delaying a Transition
lessons.content: The `transition-delay` property lets you specify a wait time before the transition begins.

lessons.title: Animate an element's opacity, but wait 1 second before starting the animation.

lessons.instruction: Use the `transition` shorthand to set a 0.3s ease-out animation.

lessons.title: Animation Artist! 🎨
lessons.content: You now have fine-grained control over your transitions, allowing you to create animations with unique personality and timing.

lessons.title: Multi-Step Animations
lessons.content: While `transition` is great for simple A-to-B state changes, `@keyframes` let you define complex, multi-step animations.

lessons.title: Defining `@keyframes`
lessons.content: You define a `@keyframes` rule with a name. Inside, you define styles at different percentage points of the animation, from `0%` (or `from`) to `100%` (or `to`).

lessons.title: Define keyframes named 'fade-in' that animate opacity from 0 to 1.

lessons.question: What is the keyword to start a keyframe definition?

lessons.title: The `animation` Property
lessons.content: To apply the keyframes to an element, you use the `animation` property, specifying the name, duration, and other settings.

lessons.title: Apply the 'fade-in' animation to a div, making it last 2 seconds.
Animation Sub-properties
lessons.content: Like `transition`, `animation` is a shorthand for properties like `animation-iteration-count` (e.g., `infinite`), `animation-direction` (e.g., `alternate`), and `animation-fill-mode`.

lessons.title: Create a pulsing animation that scales an element up and down infinitely.
lessons.expectedAnswer:
@keyframes pulse { 0% { transform: scale(1); } 50% { transform: scale(1.1); } 100% { transform: scale(1); } }
.heart { animation: pulse 1.5s infinite; }
blocks:
@keyframes pulse { 0% { transform: scale(1); } 50% { transform: scale(1.1); } 100% { transform: scale(1); } }
.heart { animation: pulse 1.5s infinite; }

lessons.title: CSS Animator! 🎬
lessons.content: You can now create complex, cinematic animations using only CSS. This is a powerful tool for grabbing user attention and creating delightful experiences.

lessons.title: Mastering Flexbox Alignment
lessons.content: Flexbox provides a powerful set of properties for aligning items along both the main and cross axes. Let's master them.

lessons.title: `justify-content` Revisited
lessons.content: `justify-content` aligns items along the main axis. We know `center`, `flex-start`, and `flex-end`. Other values include `space-between`, `space-around`, and `space-evenly`.

lessons.title: Distribute items with equal spacing around them.

lessons.question: Which value places the first item at the start, the last at the end, and distributes the rest evenly?

lessons.title: `align-items` Revisited
lessons.content: `align-items` aligns items along the cross axis. Besides `center`, `flex-start`, and `flex-end`, there's also `stretch` (the default) and `baseline`.

lessons.title: Align all flex items to the top of the container.
`align-content`
lessons.content: When you have wrapped flex lines (with `flex-wrap: wrap`), `align-content` is used to distribute the space between the lines, similar to how `justify-content` works.

lessons.title: For a wrapped container, center all the lines of items vertically.
lessons.expectedAnswer: .container { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; align-content: center; }
blocks: .container { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; align-content: center; }

lessons.title: Overriding with `align-self`
lessons.content: You can override the `align-items` value for a single flex item by applying `align-self` directly to it.

lessons.title: In a centered container, make one specific item align to the end.
Flexible Sizing
lessons.content: Flexbox provides properties to control how items grow and shrink to fill available space, making them truly 'flexible'.

lessons.title: `flex-grow`
lessons.content: `flex-grow` is a unitless value that dictates how much of the available space an item should take up. A value of `1` means 'take up an equal share'.

lessons.title: Make three child divs share the container space equally.
Make a main content area take up twice as much space as a sidebar.
`flex-shrink`
lessons.content: `flex-shrink` controls how much an item should shrink if there isn't enough space. The default is `1`. A value of `0` prevents shrinking.

lessons.title: Prevent a logo from shrinking in a flex container.
`flex-basis`
lessons.content: `flex-basis` defines the default size of an element before the remaining space is distributed. It's like a more flexible `width`.

lessons.title: Give flex items an ideal starting width of 200px.
The `flex` Shorthand
lessons.content: The `flex` property is a shorthand for `flex-grow`, `flex-shrink`, and `flex-basis` in that order. `flex: 1 0 250px;` is a common pattern.

lessons.title: Use the flex shorthand to create a flexible item that won't shrink.
Mastering CSS Grid
lessons.content: CSS Grid is a 2D layout system that gives you precise control over both rows and columns simultaneously.

lessons.title: The `fr` Unit
lessons.content: The `fr` (fractional) unit is designed for Grid. It represents a fraction of the available space in the grid container. `1fr 1fr` creates two equal columns.

lessons.title: Create a three-column layout where the middle column is twice as wide as the sides.
The `repeat()` Function
lessons.content: The `repeat()` function is a convenient way to define multiple tracks. `repeat(12, 1fr)` creates a 12-column grid.

lessons.title: Create a grid with 4 equal columns using `repeat()`.

lessons.question: What does `repeat(3, 100px)` create?

lessons.title: The `gap` Property
lessons.content: The `gap` property (shorthand for `row-gap` and `column-gap`) defines the size of the gutters between grid tracks.

lessons.title: Create a grid with a 20px gap between all items.
`minmax()`
lessons.content: The `minmax(min, max)` function defines a size range. This is great for responsive design, e.g., `minmax(200px, 1fr)` means 'be at least 200px, but grow to fill'.

lessons.title: Create a responsive column that's at least 300px wide.
Line-Based Placement
lessons.content: The lines that form the grid are numbered, starting from 1. You can place items precisely using these line numbers.

lessons.title: `grid-column` and `grid-row`
lessons.content: These properties are shorthands for `grid-column-start`/`end` and `grid-row-start`/`end`. `grid-column: 1 / 3;` makes an item start on line 1 and end on line 3.

lessons.title: In a 4-column grid, make a header item span all 4 columns.

lessons.question: To make an item span from column line 2 to 4, you'd use...

lessons.title: The `span` Keyword
lessons.content: You can also specify how many tracks an item should span. `grid-column: span 2;` makes the item take up two column tracks.

lessons.title: Make a 'featured' item start in column 2 and span 3 columns.
Named Grid Areas
lessons.content: A more intuitive way to build layouts is by naming areas with `grid-template-areas` on the parent, and then assigning items to those areas with `grid-area`.

lessons.title: Create a classic header, sidebar, content, footer layout with named areas.

lessons.instruction: Assign the main content to the 'main' grid area.

lessons.title: Grid Architect! 🏙️
lessons.content: You can now build entire, complex page layouts with CSS Grid, one of the most powerful and essential tools in a modern front-end developer's toolkit.

lessons.title: What is Responsive Design?
lessons.content: Responsive Web Design (RWD) is an approach that makes your web pages render well on a variety of devices and screen sizes, from small phones to large desktops.

lessons.title: The Viewport Meta Tag
lessons.content: The first step is always to include the viewport meta tag in your HTML `<head>`. `<meta name='viewport' content='width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0'>`.

lessons.question: What is the purpose of the viewport meta tag?
options: To control the layout viewport on mobile browsers
lessons.correct: To control the layout viewport on mobile browsers

lessons.title: Fluid Grids
lessons.content: Instead of fixed pixel widths, use relative units like percentages, `vw` (viewport width), or `fr` in Grid layouts. This allows your layout to stretch and shrink fluidly.

lessons.title: Flexible Images
lessons.content: A common practice to make images responsive is to give them `max-width: 100%;` and `height: auto;`. This ensures they never overflow their container but maintain their aspect ratio.

lessons.title: Write the CSS to make all images on a page responsive.
Mobile First
lessons.content: The 'Mobile First' approach means you design and write the base CSS for the smallest screen (mobile) first, then add complexity for larger screens using media queries.

lessons.question: What is the benefit of a 'Mobile First' strategy?
options: It forces you to prioritize content and leads to cleaner code
It only works for mobile apps
lessons.correct: It forces you to prioritize content and leads to cleaner code

lessons.title: Progressive Enhancement
lessons.content: Mobile First is a form of progressive enhancement: start with a simple baseline that works everywhere, then add enhancements for capable browsers/devices.

lessons.title: Responsive Thinker! 🤔
lessons.content: You now understand the core principles behind modern responsive design. This mindset is crucial before even writing the code.

lessons.title: The Key to Responsiveness
lessons.content: Media Queries are the tool we use to apply different CSS rules based on device characteristics, most commonly the viewport width.

lessons.title: Syntax
lessons.content: A media query starts with `@media`, followed by a media type (like `screen`), and a condition in parentheses, like `(min-width: 768px)`.

lessons.title: Create a media query that applies styles only when the screen is 600px or wider.

lessons.question: What does `(min-width: 800px)` mean?
options: When the width is less than 800px
When the width is 800px or greater
lessons.correct: When the width is 800px or greater

lessons.title: Common Breakpoints
lessons.content: While they can be anything, common 'breakpoints' for changing layouts are around 600px (tablet), 900px (small desktop), and 1200px (large desktop).

lessons.title: Make a `div`'s background red on small screens and blue on screens 768px and wider.
Combining Queries
lessons.content: You can combine conditions with `and`, and you can provide comma-separated lists to apply the same styles for different queries.

lessons.title: Apply styles only for screens between 600px and 900px wide.

lessons.instruction: Apply styles for screens smaller than 500px.

lessons.title: Responsive Ruler! 📏
lessons.content: Media queries are your primary tool for implementing responsive designs. You can now make your layouts adapt perfectly to any screen.

lessons.title: Common Responsive Patterns
lessons.content: There are several common, reusable patterns for making layouts responsive.

lessons.title: The 'Column Drop' Pattern
lessons.content: In this pattern, a multi-column layout on desktop 'drops' to a single column on mobile, with columns stacking vertically. This is a classic use for Flexbox or Grid.

lessons.title: Create a 2-column flexbox layout that stacks on screens smaller than 700px.
The 'Mostly Fluid' Pattern
lessons.content: This pattern uses a fluid grid, but adds margins on larger screens to constrain the main content to a maximum width for better readability.

lessons.title: Create a container that is 90% wide, but no wider than 1200px, and is centered.
Responsive Grids with `auto-fit`
lessons.content: CSS Grid can create magic responsive columns. `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));` creates columns that are at least 250px wide and automatically wrap.

lessons.title: Create a responsive gallery grid using `auto-fit`.
lessons.expectedAnswer: .gallery { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }
blocks: .gallery { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }

lessons.question: What is the benefit of the `auto-fit` pattern?
options: It doesn't require any media queries
lessons.correct: It doesn't require any media queries

lessons.title: Off-Canvas Navigation
lessons.content: A common mobile pattern is to hide the main navigation off-screen, and show it when a user clicks a 'hamburger' menu icon. This requires some JavaScript to toggle a class.

lessons.title: Layout Leader! 👑
lessons.content: You are now familiar with the most important and widely used responsive layout patterns on the web.

lessons.title: Readable Text on All Screens
lessons.content: Responsive typography ensures your text is legible and well-proportioned on any device.

lessons.title: Relative Font Sizes
lessons.content: Use relative units like `rem` and `em` for font sizes instead of `px`. This allows all text to scale proportionally if the user changes their browser's base font size.

lessons.question: What is the `rem` unit relative to?

lessons.title: Set a base font size on the `html` element, then use `rem` for a heading.
The `clamp()` Function
lessons.content: The `clamp(MIN, IDEAL, MAX)` function is a modern way to create fluid typography. It sets a font size that grows with the viewport but doesn't go below the MIN or above the MAX.

lessons.title: Create a fluid heading font size using `clamp()`.

lessons.question: In `clamp(1rem, 4vw, 2rem)`, what is `4vw`?

lessons.title: Line Length
lessons.content: For readability, a line of text shouldn't be too long. A good range is 45-75 characters. Use `max-width` on your text containers to control this.

lessons.title: Constrain the width of a paragraph for better readability.
lessons.expectedAnswer: p { max-width: 65ch; /* 'ch' is a unit for character width */ }
blocks: p { max-width: 65ch; /* 'ch' is a unit for character width */ }

lessons.title: Typography Titan! ✒️
lessons.content: You can now create text that is not only beautiful but also perfectly readable and accessible on any screen size.

lessons.title: Organizing Large Stylesheets
lessons.content: In large projects, CSS can become messy and hard to maintain. CSS architecture provides methodologies for keeping it organized.

lessons.title: What is BEM?
lessons.content: BEM (Block, Element, Modifier) is a popular and simple naming convention that makes your CSS more readable and less prone to conflicts.

lessons.title: Block
lessons.content: A Block is a standalone component, like `.card`, `.nav`, or `.form`. It's the root of the component.

lessons.title: Element
lessons.content: An Element is a part of a block that has no standalone meaning. It's named with the block name, two underscores, and the element name, like `.card__title`.

lessons.title: Write a BEM class for the image inside a `.card` block.

lessons.question: What is the correct BEM syntax for an element?

lessons.title: Modifier
lessons.content: A Modifier is a flag on a block or element that changes its appearance or state. It's named with two hyphens, like `.card--featured` or `.card__button--disabled`.

lessons.title: Write a BEM class for a large, primary button.

lessons.question: You have a `.form__input`. How would you write a modifier for its error state?

lessons.title: CSS Architect! 🏛️
lessons.content: You've learned a professional methodology for writing scalable and maintainable CSS. This is a critical skill for working on large projects or with a team.

lessons.title: Advanced CSS Review
lessons.content: You have learned the most powerful tools in modern CSS, from advanced selectors and animations to responsive design and architecture.

Which selector targets a `

` that is an immediate sibling after an `

`?
How do you declare a global CSS variable for a primary color?
To flip a card over, which transform would you use?
The `@keyframes` rule is used for...
To make flex items wrap onto new lines, you use...
In a 'Mobile First' approach, your media queries will mostly use...
In BEM, what does `.card__header--large` represent?

lessons.title: Ready for Mastery
lessons.content: You have all the HTML and CSS knowledge needed to build beautiful, responsive, and professional websites from scratch. The next step is to add complex logic with JavaScript.

lessons.title: CSS Master! 🏅
lessons.content: Congratulations! You have achieved a master's understanding of CSS. You can bring any design to life in the browser.
